1.headline: Some people have to grow up before their time.
1.fortune: Some people are forced to grow up before they are ready. Maybe you are carrying the weight of a decision you never felt prepared to make. Before looking for someone to blame, ask what support was missing and what help could make a difference now. Responsibility does not have to mean facing everything alone.
1.history: One of the earliest known recordings by teenage Tupac and his friends in Baltimore, this song addresses teenage pregnancy, responsibility, and social pressure. Years later, he would revisit the concern more tragically in 'Brenda’s Got a Baby.' The 1987 date comes from specialist archives, not an official release from that year.

2.headline: Waiting for someone to discover your talent?
2.fortune: Are you waiting for someone to discover your talent? That day may never arrive on its own. Sometimes you have to step forward and show people what you can do. But making noise is not enough: what remains after the excitement fades is the quality of your work. Being noticed is the beginning, not the finish line.
2.history: This track survives on a cappella demo tapes by the teenage Baltimore group Born Busy. Performing as MC New York, Tupac trades energetic call-and-response verses with his friend Ace Rocker. The point was to display skill, excite a crowd, and compete musically rather than deliver a detailed political argument.

3.headline: Sometimes a rival shows you how ready you really are.
3.fortune: Competition can reveal what you are capable of. Just be careful not to turn your entire life into a mission to defeat everybody else. If proving superiority becomes the only goal, you might forget the joy of making something worthwhile. Let competition push you forward, but choose a destination beyond your opponents.
3.history: This a cappella performance by Tupac and Ace Rocker dates to their Born Busy period. It centers on showing off rap skills in the competitive hip-hop culture of the 1980s and resembles a verbal battle between local crews. The approximate 1988 date is drawn from documentation of Tupac's teenage tapes.

4.headline: Not everything that catches your eye deserves your pursuit.
4.fortune: Not everything that catches your attention is worth chasing, especially when someone else's feelings and trust are involved. Something exciting may be tempting you right now, but attractive and right are not the same thing. Some choices taste sweet for a few minutes and reveal their true cost much later.
4.history: In this early Born Busy performance, Tupac and Ace Rocker explore attraction, relationships, and romantic rivalry. The known recording is incomplete and a cappella. Its story should therefore not be described with the certainty we would apply to a finished, officially released song.

5.headline: Nobody may see the work you do offstage.
5.fortune: Nobody may notice the hours you put in behind the scenes. From the outside, success looks sudden; from the inside, it is repetition and countless ordinary days. If you need applause after every effort, you may quit during the hardest stretch. What you build every day matters more than what you show once.
5.history: The title appears on an old Born Busy tape list, dated July 12, 1988 by a research archive. The archive describes its theme as the group's dedication to music. As a reliable full lyric transcription was not found in the cited material, this reflection draws only on that documented description.
5.details: 2Pac | July 12, 1988 | Born Busy tape, archival date

6.headline: You are not the only one building this success.
6.fortune: You are not the only person making this success possible. Someone beside you may get little recognition, yet without them everything would change. Think about the people working behind the scenes, not just the one standing in the spotlight. Some of the real heroes never hold the microphone.
6.history: A Born Busy-era tribute to the group's DJ, Gerard Young, known as DJ Plain Terror. In hip-hop culture of that period, the DJ was as important to a live performance as the rapper. Complete lyrics are not readily verifiable; the fortune is based on the track's documented role in the group's archive.
6.details: 2Pac | c. 1988 | Dedicated to DJ Plain Terror

7.headline: Sometimes you fall for the idea of someone.
7.fortune: Sometimes you fall harder for the person you imagine than for the person you actually know. In fantasy, everything unfolds just as you wish; real life asks questions and catches you off guard. If your heart is caught up in someone, ask how much you truly know. Imagination is beautiful, but it cannot replace understanding.
7.history: In an early collaboration with Ryan D, Tupac tells a playful story about infatuation, nervousness around a crush, and the line between dreams and reality. The recording is associated with the One Nation Emcees period around 1989. It reveals a humorous, romantic side of Tupac before fame.
7.details: 2Pac | c. 1989 | One Nation Emcees, unofficial release

8.headline: Trying to look unbeatable can become its own trap.
8.fortune: If your whole message is 'nobody can beat me,' you might care too much about what others think. Confidence matters, but confidence built entirely on comparisons makes every new rival a threat. Improve your craft until the work speaks for itself. Being resilient is not the same as pretending you cannot lose.
8.history: An early competitive rap recording. One version with Ryan D is associated with One Nation Emcees, while another was later recorded with Strictly Dope. Tupac and his collaborators use wordplay and exaggerated bravado to challenge rivals. The Strictly Dope version appeared later on the Beginnings compilation.

9.headline: The biggest barrier may be the one you stopped noticing.
9.fortune: Maybe the greatest obstacle in your life has become so familiar that you no longer see it. Ask which rule, expectation, or accepted story has quietly narrowed your choices. You cannot break every barrier alone, but you can begin by naming it. Freedom starts with difficult questions.
9.history: Rooted in the political legacy of the Black Panther movement and experiences of racial discrimination in the United States, the song challenges promises of equality and the 'American Dream.' Tupac's mother, Afeni Shakur, was a political activist. Early versions date to the late 1980s; a Strictly Dope version was released later.

10.headline: Are you trusting your tools more than your talent?
10.fortune: What if you have begun to trust a tool, an opportunity, or someone standing beside you more than your own ability? One day that support might disappear. Only then may you discover which strength truly belongs to you. The thing that makes you capable is not always the thing you expect.
10.history: In this humorous track, Tupac misplaces his microphone before a rap contest and panics, eventually realizing he can still perform without it. The story unfolds through dialogue with friends. It is an early Strictly Dope recording later issued in a compilation of his beginnings.

11.headline: Being heard starts with knowing more, not shouting louder.
11.fortune: If people do not take you seriously, your first response need not be raising your voice. Learn more, understand more deeply, and surround yourself with people who broaden your thinking. Knowledge alone will not remake the world, but it makes it harder for others to think in your place. Do not underestimate your mind.
11.history: Tupac and Strictly Dope address education, history, solidarity, and resistance to social constraints. The track was recorded before his first official solo album, though its exact recording date is uncertain. Released later on Beginnings, it shows the young rapper's educational and protest-minded side.

12.headline: An ordinary day can become a lifelong memory.
12.fortune: Life does not wait for something spectacular before it starts to mean something. A normal day with friends, a familiar street, a game, or an unexpected conversation can stay with you for years. If you are always waiting for 'later,' you may be missing today. Most memories are made without warning.
12.history: The song depicts everyday youth experiences: time off school, hanging out, friends, and small street rivalries. In the Strictly Dope version, Tupac and Ray Tyson sound very different from his later angrier material. It belongs to the pre-debut period and was officially released years afterward.

13.headline: Not every powerful feeling excuses a choice.
13.fortune: Sometimes you want something that could cost another person their trust. Your feelings may be real, but that does not automatically make every action right. Before you call it love, ask who could get hurt. Some attachments demand more honesty than courage.
13.history: Tupac sings about falling for his best friend's girlfriend, torn between personal desire and loyalty. Ray Tyson also contributes to the romantic narrative. An early Strictly Dope recording released later on Beginnings, it shows the younger Tupac experimenting with emotional storytelling.

14.headline: A glamorous story can hide a much harder reality.
14.fortune: The dazzling image around a relationship may conceal its reality. Perhaps you know someone only through gossip or the identity they project. Behind that image may be loneliness, need, or a struggle for power. Before judging or falling in love, hear the whole story. People are more complicated than the rumors about them.
14.history: Tupac and Ray Tyson tell Minnie's story in a tone that shifts between humor and bitterness: unstable relationships, social climbing, poverty, and violence. Part of the early Strictly Dope recordings, it shows Tupac exploring complex characters long before he became famous.

15.headline: Sometimes the room has judged you before you speak.
15.fortune: Sometimes people decide what you are capable of before you even enter a room. You do not need to answer every assumption with a long explanation. Do your work well, but do not let proving yourself turn into a permanent feud with everyone else. The strongest reply is not always the loudest.
15.history: 'Static' comes from Tupac's transition toward professional music and appears as Mix 1 and Mix 2 on the Beginnings compilation. Its tone is aggressive and competitive. Because the versions share a title and central theme, they count as one fortune here; exact recording dates are not fully established.
15.details: 2Pac | c. 1990-1991 | Two mixes of one track

16.headline: Success can reveal what people really want from you.
16.fortune: People sometimes change their behavior the moment things start going your way. Someone who ignored you yesterday may suddenly act like your closest friend. You do not have to distrust everyone, but learn to tell affection for you from interest in your new position. Fame does not always change people; sometimes it reveals their motives.
16.history: Released in 1991 by Digital Underground, this lively group song was among Tupac's first commercial appearances. In his verse, he jokes about how people treat him differently as his profile grows. The track also appeared in the film Nothing but Trouble. The recording is generally dated to late 1990.

17.headline: Don't judge me before you know me
17.fortune: It's exhausting when people have already judged you before you speak. Your appearance, age, or past may matter more to some people than the truth. You don't have to limit yourself to the picture they've made of you. But don't let your anger at those judgments control your choices either. You are more than the label they give you.
17.history: The opening track of 2Pacalypse Now, an album recorded between March and August 1991 and released that November. Tupac speaks about a young Black man's experience of policing and prejudice. In a press biography from that year, he said he performed the track in one take, drawing on his own experience.

18.headline: A blocked path isn't always the end
18.fortune: Sometimes it feels as though every direction leads to the same wall. Before blaming yourself for not getting somewhere, look at which obstacles are really within your control and which have been imposed from outside. Positive thinking won't open every lock. Some cages first need to be called by their real names.
18.history: Tupac's first solo single from 2Pacalypse Now addresses police pressure and restricted opportunities in poor neighborhoods. In an official 1991 interview, he explained that being 'trapped' meant restrictions beyond a physical prison. The track was released with Shock G's participation.

19.headline: The road that looks powerful from afar may cost too much.
19.fortune: From a distance, some paths look full of power and respect. Up close, they may offer only fear and consequences nobody mentions. Before copying someone else's major decision, look at where that road actually ends. Someone you admire is not automatically a good guide for your future.
19.history: In 'Soulja's Story,' Tupac tells a dark narrative about violence, policing, prison, and a younger brother imitating an older brother involved in crime. In his 1991 album commentary, the younger brother tries to free the older one and loses his life. It is the third track on 2Pacalypse Now.

20.headline: Anger can reveal what matters, but it should not run your life.
20.fortune: After being treated unfairly again and again, polite words may start to feel pointless. Your anger can show what you care about. But if it makes every decision for you, it may take away the very thing you wanted: control over your own life. Anger is understandable; surrendering your future to it is another matter.
20.history: The fourth track on 2Pacalypse Now protests racial discrimination and police harassment in blunt language. In 1991 press materials, Tupac described police threats against members of Digital Underground in San Francisco as one inspiration. The recording captures his outspoken political anger at the start of his solo career.

21.headline: How long will people mistake your silence for consent?
21.fortune: How long are people going to mistake your silence for agreement? Anger is natural when someone repeatedly crosses your boundaries. But the moment anger replaces choice, the thing hurting you may gain control of your life. You have every right to protest. Just do not let the protest destroy what you meant to protect.
21.history: Through a tense narrative, Tupac addresses police violence and the anger of young Black Americans. In a 1991 interview, he called the track an outlet for his frustration with police behavior. It appeared on his debut album, where political rage sometimes mixes with violent imagery.

22.headline: Some people would rather you never asked questions.
22.fortune: Some people are more comfortable when you do not ask questions. Hearing only one side of history can make you repeat someone else's story without realizing it. Re-examine the things people call 'the way it has always been.' Learning cannot erase every pain, but it can stop someone else from deciding for you through ignorance.
22.history: Tupac challenges the United States over racism and the erasure of Black history, presenting education as resistance. He mentions Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. and explains his own interpretation of the acronym N.I.G.G.A. The song highlights the political, educational side of his debut album.

23.headline: You cannot build everything with ready-made tools.
23.fortune: Maybe you have been waiting for perfect circumstances: the right people, enough money, or a chance with no risks. Some abilities emerge only when you have to work without the tools you usually depend on. What looks like a shortage today might show you what you can really do.
23.history: On 'Something Wicked,' Tupac focuses more on rap technique and performance energy. In 1991, he explained that he wanted to prove they could make beats and perform without relying on pre-existing samples. Unlike many political tracks on the album, this song stands out for its approach to music-making.

24.headline: Revenge rarely settles an old debt.
24.fortune: Revenge does not always pay off an old debt; it can create a new one. Someone may have betrayed you, and now you want them to feel exactly the same pain. Think about the end of that cycle: what will actually be repaired afterward? Some victories are only another name for the same old defeat.
24.history: Tupac and Stretch play violent street characters in this track. The plot moves from robbery and pursuit to revenge, gunfire, and confrontation with police. Unlike some socially focused songs on the album, it depicts criminal violence directly. The narrator should not be equated with Tupac's actual life without evidence.
24.details: 2Pac feat. Stretch | Recorded 1991 | Released November 12, 1991 | 2Pacalypse Now

25.headline: Real friends are not only there for the good days.
25.fortune: Real friends are not always found in your happiest moments. Life gets busy and old relationships can slip onto an endless 'later' list. Yet a simple call might mean much more to someone than the few minutes it costs you. As you grow, do not lose the people who were there before anybody knew your name.
25.history: Tupac contrasts loyalty to longtime friends with fame and an increasingly busy schedule. In an interview about his debut, he said a show or movie should never make him forget real friends. One of the three singles associated with 2Pacalypse Now, the track shows a more affectionate side of him.

26.headline: Behind every painful story, a hidden truth
26.fortune: Behind some mistakes is someone nobody came to help. Judging from a distance is easy; seeing the fear, poverty, and loneliness behind a decision is much harder. Today you may meet someone who needs to be heard more than they need advice. Before asking, 'Why did they do that?' ask, 'Who was there for them?'
26.history: 'Brenda's Got a Baby' tells the story of a very young girl facing abuse, pregnancy, and poverty. Tupac said a disturbing news report about a teenage girl's life inspired the song. One of his earliest well-known examples of social storytelling, it addresses vulnerable children and the failure of support networks.

27.headline: You are bigger than the role others expect you to play.
27.fortune: Just because everyone expects a certain version of you does not mean you have to stay that person. You may be known as the funny one in one group and the serious one in another. If you keep performing those roles against your feelings, you may lose yourself. Your character is bigger than other people's labels.
27.history: Tupac explained that 'The Lunatic' had been one of his underground rap nicknames, referring to quick shifts in behavior. With Stretch, he builds an unpredictable, exaggerated persona. The song is best read as a performance of an artistic identity, not a psychological diagnosis.
27.details: 2Pac feat. Stretch | Recorded 1991 | Released November 12, 1991 | 2Pacalypse Now

28.headline: You do not have to sound like everyone else to belong.
28.fortune: You do not need to imitate everyone else's voice just to be accepted. Maybe you have something to say that could cost you approval. Before going silent, ask what scares you more: being wrong or upsetting others. Disagreeing with the crowd does not guarantee you are right, but agreement does not prove it either. Dare to think.
28.history: Tupac treated the track as a statement of his rebellious artistic identity. In a 1991 interview, he described himself as someone who often protested more loudly than others. The lyrics criticize the media, censorship, and police violence. Ray Luv and Shock G are credited collaborators.
28.details: 2Pac feat. Ray Luv & Shock G | Recorded 1991 | Released November 12, 1991 | 2Pacalypse Now

29.headline: Someone can be absent even while standing beside you.
29.fortune: Some absences hurt even when the person is physically present. Responsibility is more than having your name attached to someone's life: it means paying attention when they truly need you. Someone close may be asking for nothing more than your presence. Half-hearted care is not always harmless; its effects can last for years.
29.history: Closing his debut album, Tupac joins several harsh stories about parental neglect, addiction, abuse, and abandoned children. He described the track as an answer to songs that glamorize dangerous lifestyles. Its main concern is the cost of adult choices to children who never had a say in them.
29.details: 2Pac feat. Angelique & Poppi | Recorded 1991 | Released November 12, 1991 | 2Pacalypse Now

30.headline: Your voice deserves to be heard too
30.fortune: Some things seem to go unheard when you say them alone. Maybe you've been waiting for someone else to speak first and name the problem everyone can see. But one voice can break other people's silence. Before bringing people together, make sure you know exactly what change you want. A shout cannot take the place of a direction.
30.history: The first single from Tupac's second album. In interview notes from the time, he described it as a call for uprising and unity, responding to continuing discrimination after the 1992 Los Angeles riots. Compared with his first album, Tupac faced greater fame and media pressure, and his political voice sounded sharper.

31.headline: Sometimes people judge you before you get to speak.
31.fortune: Sometimes a verdict is passed before you say a word. You may be tempted to respond, especially when the person judging you holds power. But not every reply deserves all your energy. Decide whether you are trying to clarify the truth or simply prove you are nobody's inferior. Those are not always the same goal.
31.history: This interlude responds to criticism of Tupac and rap music by Dan Quayle, then U.S. vice president. Tupac explained in an official interview that he placed excerpts of Quayle's statements beside responses drawn from his own interviews. It captures the young artist's conflict with political and media power.

32.headline: When you point a finger, where are the others pointing?
32.fortune: When you point a finger at someone else, where are the others pointing? You may be condemning someone for a fault you also carry in a smaller form. That does not excuse their mistakes. It reminds you that judging is easy, while facing your own role in the story takes much more courage.
32.history: In discussion of his second album, Tupac described 'Point the Finga' as a response to people who portrayed him as evil while ignoring their own wrongdoing. He turns their accusations back on the critics with sharp language. The track reflects the strain of fame and media scrutiny in 1992.
32.details: 2Pac | Recorded 1992 | Released February 16, 1993 | Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z...

33.headline: Not every cause is worth losing your life over.
33.fortune: Do not fight for everything; some things are not worth losing yourself over. Pride, jealousy, or a stranger's words can push a person toward an irreversible decision. When you decide to stand your ground, ask whether the cause gives your life meaning or just briefly soothes your anger. The difference could change everything.
33.history: In this interlude, Tupac recalls the death of Latasha Harlins and a child killed in a shooting near one of his performances. In his commentary, he said freedom is worth fighting for, unlike jealousy or pointless violence. Released in 1993, the piece criticizes needless deaths despite its provocative title.

34.headline: When someone wants to silence you, ask what they fear.
34.fortune: If someone wants to shut you up, ask which words frighten them. Their harsh reaction may mean you have touched a sensitive point. But freedom to speak does not absolve you of thinking about your words' effects. An independent voice is not merely loud; it takes responsibility for what it says.
34.history: Tupac joins Ice Cube and Ice-T to oppose censorship of rap music. He described the song as the three artists' final statement on attempts to restrict their expression. The collaboration links him to established protest-rap figures. It is track five on the original 16-track album and should not be omitted.
34.details: 2Pac feat. Ice Cube & Ice-T | Recorded 1992 | Released February 16, 1993 | Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z...

35.headline: Fighting for justice and hurting people are different things.
35.fortune: When you feel there is no way to be heard, retaliation can look appealing. But revenge seldom solves the problem; it usually draws more people into it. Maybe it is time to break the cycle rather than answer with your opponent's methods. Demanding justice is not the same as causing harm.
35.history: 'Souljah's Revenge' conceptually follows 'Soulja's Story' from Tupac's debut. He presented it as a response to efforts to ban his music. The lyrics describe clashes with police and make harsh accusations against power structures. The song's violent narrative should be distinguished from verified real-world statements or events.
35.details: 2Pac | Recorded 1992 | Released February 16, 1993 | Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z...

36.headline: Not everything is black and white.
36.fortune: Not everything is black and white, even when you feel absolutely certain you are right. The person standing against you may not have told the whole story, or you may see only a fragment. Look once more from another angle before passing a final judgment. Complexity does not mean your boundaries no longer matter.
36.history: With Deadly Threat, Tupac uses an aggressive, competitive tone to discuss reputation, fame, and street codes. In his commentary, he suggested that not every issue can be understood in stark black-and-white terms. The track blends rap bravado, threats, and distrust in relationships.
36.details: 2Pac feat. Deadly Threat | Recorded 1992 | Released February 16, 1993 | Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z...

37.headline: Feeling tired does not mean you have failed.
37.fortune: Being exhausted is not always the same as giving up. Some days, reaching the evening is a small victory. You do not owe everyone a full explanation of your struggles, but you do not have to pretend everything is fine either. If pressure has lasted a long time, asking for help is not weakness. Nobody should have to endure everything alone.
37.history: Tupac said he wrote this song about everyday struggles so listeners could recognize themselves in it. In his circle, 'I'm struggling' had become a familiar answer to 'How are you?' Featuring Live Squad, it portrays difficult lives without promising easy success, and belongs to his 1992 recording period.
37.details: 2Pac feat. Live Squad | Recorded 1992 | Released February 16, 1993 | Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z...

38.headline: Some comebacks need no explanation.
38.fortune: Some comebacks speak for themselves. Maybe you failed once, stepped away, or heard people declare you finished. You do not have to spend your life convincing them otherwise. If something still matters to you, return and continue, not to punish their judgment but because you still have something to say. A comeback only matters if you move forward.
38.history: 'Guess Who's Back' is an energetic declaration of Tupac's return. In brief comments from 1992, he said others wanted him to withdraw, but he had no intention of leaving. The song emerged after his controversial debut and as his acting in Juice was bringing him wider recognition.
38.details: 2Pac | Recorded 1992 | Released February 16, 1993 | Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z...

39.headline: Success does not require abandoning your roots.
39.fortune: When you succeed, you do not have to leave your past at the door. You may enter a room where everybody expects you to act like them. Growth means having new choices, not erasing everything that made you. Just do not confuse loyalty to your roots with an obligation to repeat old mistakes. You can move forward and remain yourself.
39.history: Tupac mentions Oakland, his path from the streets to movies, and other contemporary artists. In album notes, he said he represented young Black people and his beliefs. 'Representin’ 93' reflects a period when his rising fame intersected with an identity deeply rooted in his community.
39.details: 2Pac | Recorded 1992 | Released February 16, 1993 | Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z...

40.headline: Being strong doesn't mean being alone
40.fortune: Does someone still standing necessarily mean they're doing well? A woman around you may carry more each day than you can see and receive less respect than she deserves. Instead of admiring her resilience from a distance, consider what would actually lighten her load. Sometimes respect shows in everyday behavior, rather than beautiful words.
40.history: Tupac wrote this song for women who had connected with the story of 'Brenda's Got a Baby.' He sings about respect for Black women and mothers, and the pressure of social inequality. Released on his second album alongside its angrier tracks, it is one of his clearest expressions of social empathy.

43.headline: Not every kind of attention is love
43.fortune: Being attractive to others doesn't always mean knowing how to be in a relationship. Maybe you've confused freedom with avoiding every commitment, or others expect something you don't want to accept. Being honest about what you want is better than making a promise you don't intend to keep. You have the right to enjoy yourself; you don't have the right to play with people.
43.history: With members of Digital Underground, Tupac sings about casual relationships and sexual pleasure on this upbeat, dance-friendly track. He explicitly said it wasn't moral advice, but a description of behavior he saw among touring artists. Its contrast with 'Keep Ya Head Up' is part of the well-known contradictions of his second album.

44.headline: Some absences never quite go away
44.fortune: No explanation can fill the space some people leave. Maybe you've spent years waiting for an apology from someone whose absence changed your life. You have the right to be angry about that absence. But you don't have to keep your whole future waiting for their return. One person's absence shouldn't become your permanent definition of yourself.
44.history: Tupac connected this song to his own father and to fathers who leave their families and may later return. In commentary published with the album, he spoke about his unfamiliarity with a father's role. The song shows anger and deprivation from a child's perspective, while also bringing in the voice of the other side of the relationship.

51.headline: Some losses stay with us for a long time
51.fortune: Missing someone doesn't always show itself in tears. After someone was gone, maybe you worked, joked, or even became angry, then wondered why you weren't grieving like everyone else. There is no single shape for loss. Just don't let the anger left behind by grief hurt the people still living. You don't have to forget in order to carry on.
51.history: Made in memory of the group's late friend Kato. Tupac, Big Syke, and other Thug Life members, joined by Nate Dogg, speak of grief, memories of friendship, and the desire for revenge. The title asks how long sorrow lasts, while also expressing a bitter worry about who will remember them after their own deaths.

58.headline: When the world is against you, don't lose yourself
58.fortune: Being alone doesn't always mean you're in the wrong. Maybe lately everything seems to go against your plans and nobody understands how you feel. You can use that feeling to keep moving, but you don't have to turn the whole world into an enemy. Even one trustworthy person can make a big difference. Being independent isn't the same as fighting alone.
58.history: The title track of Tupac's third album features Dramacydal. He speaks about police pressure, neighborhood violence, the deaths of friends, and distrust, but ends by encouraging the listener to hold on to their identity and endure. It is a clear example of the mixture of pessimism and hope in his music before his release from prison.

59.headline: There are tears nobody sees
59.fortune: Sometimes someone is still breathing but feels far more exhausted inside than they show. Maybe you've experienced several losses or worries in a row and haven't had time to grieve. You don't have to keep everything inside to prove your strength. If the pressure has become too much, talking to someone you feel safe with can be a start. Unspoken pain doesn't disappear on its own.
59.history: In 'So Many Tears,' Tupac sings about friends' deaths, childhood memories, fear, guilt, and a longing for peace. He repeatedly remembers Kato and moves between wanting to change and feeling trapped. Released on the 1995 album and later as a single, the track is far more vulnerable than his image as a fearless fighter.

64.headline: Some kinds of love take time to understand
64.fortune: Maybe the person you've complained about most has fought hardest for you. Some acts of love become visible only when it's late, or when you've tasted hardship yourself. You don't have to make the past look perfect; you can recognize both the wounds and the effort. Gratitude means seeing a person's truth more fully.
64.history: Tupac dedicated this song to his mother, Afeni Shakur, openly addressing poverty, teenage disagreements, his father's absence, and his mother's addiction. Despite those painful experiences, he honors her sacrifices. Released as a single in 1995 before his third album, 'Dear Mama' is one of his most important personal works.

67.headline: The past still has something to say
67.fortune: Not everything new has to be better than an old memory. Sometimes, while everyone competes to be more current, we forget who opened the way. Today might be a good time to return to what you first fell in love with, to learn from it rather than stay in the past. Having roots doesn't stop you from growing.
67.history: In 'Old School,' Tupac fondly remembers pioneering hip-hop artists, DJs, and the atmosphere in which rap culture took shape. Although he had become a star of a new generation, he acknowledges his debt to earlier ones. The song appears on his 1995 album and shows his appreciation of history and those who came before him.

71.headline: Succeed for yourself, not for revenge
71.fortune: Sometimes you want to succeed simply because you never want anyone to humiliate you again. Anger can be a powerful engine, but if you give it the steering wheel too, it may take you to the wrong destination. Today, ask yourself whether you're fighting for your dream or answering the past. Victory belongs to you when you've chosen it yourself.
71.history: The aggressive opening track of All Eyez on Me announces Tupac's return after prison. He speaks of ambition, threats against enemies, police, and wealth. Released in February 1996 after he joined Death Row, the album puts the image of the street fighter at the center of his new identity through this song.

75.headline: Know your own wishes apart from other people's eyes
75.fortune: When all eyes are on you, you may forget what you actually want. Other people's approval feels good, but it can come with expectations and interference. Distinguish pleasure you've chosen from a performance meant to please others. If someone wants something from you, you also have the right to set boundaries. Attention isn't always respect.
75.history: Joined by K-Ci & JoJo on this popular track, Tupac moves between sexual pleasure and responses to media and political critics. The lyrics also address the pressure of public opinion. Released on All Eyez on Me in February 1996 and later as a single, it shows the coexistence of celebration and confrontation in this period.

76.headline: Not every ally is heading where you are
76.fortune: Two people can become very powerful together without necessarily following the right path. Maybe you've found someone as daring as you are, and everyone talks about your strength together. Before taking the next step, ask yourself what this alliance creates and what it destroys. Loyalty doesn't erase responsibility for the choices you make together.
76.history: In this famous collaboration, Tupac and Snoop Doggy Dogg rap about fame, police, money, and a gangster identity. The title is an ironic reference to being 'most wanted.' From 1996's All Eyez on Me, the song showcases the shared position of Death Row's two stars.

79.headline: Life goes on, even when it hurts
79.fortune: Some people leave, and the world carries on mercilessly. Maybe you still wish time would stop on one particular day. You have the right to keep someone's memory, even when everyone else has returned to ordinary life. But moving forward isn't a betrayal of that memory. You can love someone for the rest of your life and still go on living.
79.history: In this lament for friends who were killed, Tupac pictures funerals and the fear of an early death. Alongside that bitterness, he speaks of life continuing for those left behind. Released on All Eyez on Me in 1996, it clearly shows the longing and thoughts of death present in his otherwise loud and celebratory album.

80.headline: Nobody knows your whole story
80.fortune: Tired of everyone passing judgment on you? You may really have faced unfair judgments. Still, the fact that others shouldn't define you by one mistake doesn't mean you have no responsibility. You can defend your privacy and acknowledge your own mistakes at the same time. Reject hasty judgment, without rejecting accountability.
80.history: With Rappin' 4-Tay, Tupac addresses distrust, shootings, social judgment, and spiritual accountability. The title leaves final judgment to God, but the lyrics also contain threats and pessimism. From his 1996 album, the song shows the tension between wanting to be understood and displaying violence.

82.headline: Sometimes you just need to live
82.fortune: Sometimes life needs a night of celebration rather than a long explanation. If you've been under pressure for a long time, you deserve a moment to enjoy your success. Just make sure being seen doesn't force you to keep playing the happy person. A real celebration is beautiful when you can still be yourself the next day. Joy isn't meant to hide something.
82.history: 'California Love' is Tupac and Dr. Dre's famous collaboration celebrating California and the West Coast party scene. The original single came out in late 1995, but the version on All Eyez on Me in February 1996 is a remix. To avoid duplication, the song's versions share one chapter in this project.

83.headline: People change; resentment doesn't have to follow
83.fortune: People change, sometimes without meaning to leave you behind. A friend who chooses a new path hasn't necessarily betrayed the past. You may feel hurt, but you can be happy for them without holding on to old pain. Not everyone grows at the same pace or in the same direction. Some goodbyes are gentler with forgiveness.
83.history: With Danny Boy singing, Tupac speaks about friends who took different paths through prison, religion, family, or success. Instead of threats, the song offers acceptance of growing apart and memories of the past. Released on the 1996 album, its famous video drew more attention after Tupac's death.

87.headline: Betrayal hurts most when it comes from close by
87.fortune: A wound from someone close takes longer to heal. Maybe you're still carrying words you never had the chance to say. You can express the truth of your hurt without spending your whole life proving someone else was at fault. Be careful that old anger doesn't contaminate every new relationship. Past betrayal shouldn't become the rule for future trust.
87.history: On this track, Tupac refers to the pain of betrayal, the 1994 shooting, and disagreements with people close to him, voicing personal, sharp complaints. The targets of some passages remain debated, so every detail should not be treated as settled historical fact. It appeared on the second disc of his 1996 album.

91.headline: Surviving is a victory in itself
91.fortune: When you come out of a difficult time, you want everyone to see that you endured. Maybe someone is still waiting to watch you fail. You deserve to enjoy your freedom and achievements, but your happiness doesn't have to be addressed entirely to old enemies. The best part of arriving is when you no longer need an audience.
91.history: With Big Syke and CPO, Tupac speaks about freedom, luxury cars, money, and moving beyond his time in prison. The track is particularly associated with the image of moving freely through the streets. All Eyez on Me was recorded shortly after Tupac's 1995 release and came out in February 1996.

94.headline: Being seen isn't the same as being understood
94.fortune: Being seen is different from being understood. Maybe lately it feels as though everyone has an opinion on your choices, from those closest to you to people you don't know. You don't have to answer every look, but you can't hide responsibility for your actions behind fame or pressure either. When all eyes are on you, your own gaze matters most.
94.history: On the album's title track, Tupac speaks about fame, police surveillance, enemies, and feeling under a microscope. The album title sums up his life after prison and the intense media attention around him. Released in February 1996, the song is a central track of his two-disc project.

99.headline: When anger meets faith
99.fortune: When anger and faith share one heart, making decisions becomes difficult. Maybe you want revenge while also searching for a sign of peace. Don't mistake those two voices for each other. Pain may explain your anger, but that anger doesn't have to write your future. Not every prayer is an answer to a war.
99.history: As Makaveli, Tupac draws on prayer, threats, death, hostility, and a desire for release. The religious title 'Hail Mary' sits alongside violent street imagery, creating the song's contrast. Recorded in summer 1996, it was released on the posthumous album The 7 Day Theory.

101.headline: Some cities become part of who we are
101.fortune: Sometimes a city is more than somewhere to live; it's part of your identity. You can be tired of its streets and still unable to let go of it. Home isn't always perfect. It holds memories, pain, and contradictory people. Loving a place means seeing both its goodness and its wounds.
101.history: With Val Young's vocals, Tupac speaks about Los Angeles: its neighborhoods, money, tension, and his love for the city he calls home. Recorded during the Makaveli period, the track was released after his death in November 1996. Alongside affection for the city, the lyrics reflect the tense atmosphere of rap rivalries.

107.headline: Don't cling to something that won't let you be free
107.fortune: Not every relationship we become attached to is with a person. Sometimes you think something is your only refuge while it brings you closer to danger every day. If leaving it seems impossible, maybe it's time to name that dependence honestly. Loyalty to something that destroys you isn't love.
107.history: The title deliberately leads the listener to imagine a romance, but the 'girlfriend' in Tupac's story is a metaphor for a gun. Through the image of romantic loyalty, he links violence with dependence on a weapon. Released on the 1996 Makaveli album, the track should not be read simply as a love song.

108.headline: Freedom matters more than money
108.fortune: Your bank account may have grown without making you feel any freer. If you've sacrificed sleep, peace, and important people in your life to achieve something, perhaps it's time to redefine success. Today, hold on to one thing money can't buy. Freedom means more than an open door.
108.history: On this track, Tupac pays tribute to prisoners, including political prisoners, and speaks about anxiety, fame, and the value of freedom. In the lyrics, money means less when measured against freedom. It belongs to the last album recorded during his lifetime, released after his death in November 1996.

128.headline: Love shouldn't make you lose yourself
128.fortune: Love becomes dangerous when you forget yourself to keep it. Maybe you've repeatedly done things that went against your judgment and peace of mind simply because you didn't want to lose someone. Having feelings isn't wrong, but losing every boundary can hurt you. Look at the relationship from the outside for a moment. Loving someone shouldn't mean disappearing.
128.history: Featuring Eric Williams of Blackstreet in its released version, this song addresses emotional attraction, betrayal, dependence, and decisions made for love. It samples Bobby Caldwell's 'What You Won't Do for Love.' The familiar version appeared after Tupac's death on the 1997 album and became a successful single.

138.headline: Look in the rearview mirror; don't live in it
138.fortune: Don't always look in the rearview mirror, but don't forget it either. Maybe something from the past still follows you: a mistake, a relationship, or a missed opportunity. Looking back is useful for understanding, rather than living in the same scene. Learn from what you've been through, then look ahead again. Driving with your eyes fixed behind you isn't the way out.
138.history: This collaboration between Tupac and the Outlawz appeared on the soundtrack of Gang Related in 1997. Its theme is looking back while danger and pursuit continue, and the rearview mirror metaphor fits the film's atmosphere. The recording dates from Tupac's lifetime, although the final release came after his death.

142.headline: Real love isn't measured in fear
142.fortune: Real affection doesn't demand a daily loyalty test. Maybe you love someone but constantly fear their feelings will change if you aren't successful. Unconditional love doesn't mean tolerating every behavior; it means not measuring a person's worth only by money and status. Notice where you're seen in your relationships and where you're only assessed. Being loved shouldn't be a performance reward.
142.history: A song about love and loyalty, performed by Tupac with Nanci Fletcher's vocals and released on Greatest Hits in 1998. The original vocal was recorded in 1996, while the final version was prepared after his death. Alongside the violent works of the same period, it reveals a gentler, more family-centered side of his outlook.

143.headline: Anger doesn't always get the last word
143.fortune: Anger can make you look invincible for a few minutes. What comes next? Maybe someone insulted you and you want to answer in a way everyone will remember. First ask whether you're looking for a solution or an audience. Some responses echo for years beyond the disagreement itself. Winning a fight doesn't always make life better.
143.history: Tupac's diss track featuring the Outlawz first appeared in 1996 as the companion track to the 'How Do U Want It' single, and later on Greatest Hits. The lyrics directly attack The Notorious B.I.G. and his associates. It is one of the fiercest expressions of the East Coast–West Coast hip-hop conflict of that period.

145.headline: Nothing changes unless someone wants it to
145.fortune: When everyone says, 'That's just how the world is,' ask yourself who benefits from it staying that way. Maybe you've spent a long time putting up with injustice or an unwritten rule. Change doesn't always begin with a grand decision; sometimes it starts by questioning something everyone considers normal. If something is wrong, being old doesn't make it right.
145.history: Tupac recorded the song years before its release, and the famous version came out posthumously in 1998. A piano sample from Bruce Hornsby's 'The Way It Is' gives life to a protest against racism, poverty, drugs, and police violence. It is among his best-known social and posthumous works.

172.headline: Big promises face big tests
172.fortune: The promise 'for the rest of my life' is beautiful, but people change along the way. Maybe you're still loyal to a relationship, an idea, or an image of yourself formed years ago. Loyalty matters, yet you can ask what should stay and what has the right to change. Staying true to your values doesn't always mean staying the same person.
172.history: The title track of the 2001 posthumous album finds Tupac speaking about friendship, fame, people changing, and loyalty until the end. The song also draws on pop and R&B sounds and is connected with the Outlawz. The RP Remix is a version of the same song and is not numbered as another fortune in this collection.
172.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released 2001

195.headline: Maybe you just need somewhere safe
195.fortune: Maybe what you're searching for isn't more success, just somewhere safe. A place where you don't have to explain why you're tired or be ready to defend yourself every moment. Ask yourself where, and with whom, you can truly feel at peace. Sometimes the biggest dream is one night without worry.
195.history: Tupac imagines a place of peace for people who have lived under the pressure of poverty, shootings, and death. An acoustic version with Nas and another version with Anthony Hamilton appeared on Better Dayz in 2002; both rework the same song. Its references to death and suffering are serious.

198.headline: Better days begin today
198.fortune: Better days don't start by denying today. Maybe you're tired of everyone saying, 'It'll be fine,' while the problem is still right in front of you. Hope is serious when it addresses the causes of hardship and does something to change them. You don't have to fix everything yourself, but you can choose your part. Hope isn't another name for forgetting.
198.history: On the title track of the 2002 album, Tupac speaks about drugs, murder, poverty, prison, and hope for a safer neighborhood. The album version was released with Mr. Biggs's vocals. Despite its hopefulness, the track doesn't offer a simplified or sanitized picture of street life.

209.headline: Sometimes you have to stop running
209.fortune: If you're running all day, stop once to ask what you're running from. Maybe you've been in such a hurry to save yourself that you haven't noticed which fear still follows you. Sometimes the circumstances need to change; sometimes your way of seeing them does. Aimless running won't solve either. Finding a way out begins with recognizing the danger.
209.history: Combining recorded vocals by Tupac and The Notorious B.I.G. with production by Eminem, this track appeared on the 2003 documentary soundtrack. It addresses violence, death, and life under pressure. The final combination was made after both rappers had died, rather than being a new collaboration between them.

214.headline: Before judging, see the world through their eyes
214.fortune: Before judging the next generation, look at the world you've left them. You may be angry at younger people's behavior while overlooking the fears and failures surrounding them. Blame alone doesn't bring change. Sometimes the right question isn't, 'Why did they turn out this way?' but, 'What did we give them?'
214.history: On this song, Tupac speaks about violence, racism, young people, and a wish for peace. The 2004 version, produced by Eminem, uses parts of Elton John's music and was released on Loyal to the Game. The verses and final arrangement belong to two different periods.
